problem.theorem:
2. Show that there are infinitely many pairs of positive integers $(m, n)$ such that

$$
\frac{m+1}{n}+\frac{n+1}{m}
$$
is a positive integer.

conditions: ker(phi) is the kernel of phi
rule_candidates.name: First isomorphism theorem for groups
rule_candidates.statement: If phi: G -> H is a group homomorphism, then G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).

rule_candidates.conclusion: G/N is a group and coset multiplication is well-defined.
conditions: N is a subgroup of G
rule_candidates.name: Quotient group criterion
rule_candidates.statement: If N is a normal subgroup of G, then the set of left cosets G/N forms a group under (aN)(bN) = abN.

rule_candidates.conclusion: R/I is a ring and coset operations are well-defined.
conditions: I is a two-sided ideal of R
rule_candidates.name: Quotient ring criterion
rule_candidates.statement: If I is a two-sided ideal of a ring R, then R/I is a quotient ring with operations defined on cosets.

target_node.claim: Defines S(m,n) and reduces the goal to constructing infinitely many positive-integer pairs for which S(m,n)=4.
target_node.text:
Let  

\[
S(m,n)=\frac{m+1}{n}+\frac{n+1}{m}\qquad (m ,n\in \Bbb Z_{>0}).
\]

We shall show that there are infinitely many couples \((m,n)\) with \(S(m,n)\in \Bbb Z\).
It is enough to exhibit infinitely many solutions for a single integral value of
\(S(m,n)\); we choose the value \(4\).
